overview: Cooks Coffee Company (formerly Cooks Global Foods) is a New Zealand-domiciled, NZX/AQSE (London, ticker COOK) dual-listed micro-cap franchisor of the Esquires Coffee brand, an organic/Fairtrade-positioned coffee-house concept. Its core business is the UK and Ireland franchise network (105 sites at 31 March 2026, 82 in the UK), supplemented by a small international master-franchise network (Saudi Arabia, Pakistan, Portugal, Jordan, and newly signed India and UAE agreements) and a handful of company-managed cafes inside Tesco Ireland and Dairygold supermarket sites. Reported revenue is small (NZ$12.8m FY2026) relative to the NZ$95.8m of system-wide store sales the network actually generates, because the company earns royalties/franchise fees on the vast majority of stores rather than the store sales themselves.

business_model.summary: Primarily an asset-light coffee-shop franchisor earning royalties (a percentage of franchisee store sales, reported monthly), upfront/deferred franchise and master-franchise fees (recognised over ~10-year contract terms), and coffee/consumable supply margins. A small but fast-growing minority of revenue now comes from company-managed stores (the Dairygold and Tesco Ireland partnerships), where full store sales — not just royalties — are consolidated as Group revenue, alongside the associated staff and occupancy costs. This managed-store model is capital-heavier and lower-margin than pure franchising.

revenue_streams.name: Global franchising/master-franchise & retail (NZ HQ, international royalties)

business_model.customer_type: B2B (franchisees and master franchisees who in turn serve B2C coffee-shop customers); ~250,000 customers served weekly across the UK & Ireland network
business_model.geographic_mix: UK ~52% of FY26 segment revenue, Ireland ~42% (franchising + managed cafes), New Zealand (HQ) ~3%, other international (Saudi Arabia, Pakistan, Portugal, Jordan, emerging India/UAE) ~2% of reported revenue but a larger share of system-wide sales via master-franchise agreements

competitive_position.market_position: Small niche player: Esquires' own disclosure puts its UK branded-café market share at ~0.8% of ~11,456 stores (targeting 1.9% by 2030) and Irish share at ~2.5% of ~768 stores (targeting 4.6% by 2030), versus Costa Coffee's ~38% UK share, Starbucks ~19% and Caffe Nero ~9%. Esquires is outgrowing the broader market on a percentage basis (store growth and like-for-like sales ahead of Allegra/World Coffee Portal industry benchmarks) but off a tiny base.

moat_factors.description: 100% Fairtrade and organic coffee sourcing, carbon-neutral roastery partnership, community-hub positioning differentiate from mass-market chains; genuine but a marketing angle more than a hard cost or switching-cost moat, and easily replicated by well-funded competitors.

UK Regional Developer structure (sub-territory master franchisees who recruit and support local operators) has driven above-market store growth in the Southeast of England (+39% store sales in FY26) at low capital cost to Cooks; still unproven in Scotland/Northern Ireland/West Midlands where partners are still being sought.

Focus on market towns, suburbs, housing developments and retail parks (vs city-centre/commuter locations favoured by larger chains) provided some COVID-era and post-COVID resilience against work-from-home trends.
No meaningful network effect; franchisee switching costs are limited to sunk fit-out capital and the 10-year contract term, not a durable structural moat.
Company is a sub-scale price-taker versus Costa/Starbucks/Nero on procurement, marketing spend, and property negotiating power.

weaknesses: Extreme scale disadvantage versus Costa, Starbucks, Caffe Nero and Greggs, all of which have vastly larger balance sheets and marketing budgets
Reliant on franchisee financial health and store-level execution over which Cooks has only contractual, not operational, control
Single-brand concentration (Esquires) with limited product/format diversification versus larger multi-format rivals moving into drive-thru/kiosk/convenience formats
Micro-cap status (NZ$~15-20m market cap range) limits access to capital for competing on brand investment

growth_drivers: UK & Ireland store count target of 300 by FY2034 (105 at end FY2026), fed by the Regional Developer model and new appointees in the Southwest/South Wales, with Scotland, Northern Ireland and West Midlands still to be signed
Tesco Ireland partnership (5 in-store Esquires cafes signed, first opened Nov 2025) provides a low-cost, high-footfall distribution channel that could be expanded or replicated with other retailers
Dairygold company-managed superstore cafes in Munster, Ireland — still ramping (Mallow contributed only 43 weeks in FY26) and management expects this stream to "grow significantly in FY27"

New master franchise agreements for India (signed May 2025, Sterling Coffee Houses) and the UAE (signed December 2025, minimum 50 outlets over a 10-year term) — early-stage, unproven execution but large addressable markets
Debt paydown (NZ$4.3m to NZ$2.86m in FY26) improving balance sheet flexibility for further expansion

Structural UK/Irish branded coffee market growth (Allegra/World Coffee Portal projects ~3.0% UK and ~2.4% Irish CAGR in store numbers to 2030) provides a mild secular tailwind, though Esquires is trying to grow share faster than the market

business.description: Revenue is contractually dependent on individual franchisees' store-level performance and solvency; the company has already recorded discontinued-operations losses (3 UK store closures generated a $219k H1 FY26 loss including $151k bad debts) showing franchisee failures flow directly through to Cooks' P&L.

business.risk: Revenue recognition/segment complexity obscures underlying growth
business.description: The FY2026 84-87% headline revenue increase is very substantially a function of newly consolidating company-managed store sales (Dairygold/Tesco), not organic franchise royalty growth; investors extrapolating the headline growth rate risk materially overstating the trajectory of the core franchising business (see Recent Developments for detail).

The vast majority of value is concentrated in the Esquires brand across just two core markets (UK, Ireland); a downturn in either market or reputational damage to the brand would be highly material to the whole group.

business.risk: Execution risk on new managed-store model
business.description: Company-managed stores (Dairygold, Tesco) shift Cooks from a pure capital-light franchisor to a direct operator bearing staff, occupancy and inventory risk in those locations — a different, less-proven risk profile than the franchise royalty model that has defined the business historically.
Both agreements are very recent (May 2025 and December 2025) with no meaningful trading history; execution depends entirely on third-party master franchisees the company does not control.

financial.risk: Negative shareholders' equity / thin balance sheet
financial.description: Net assets were NZ$(2.223)m at 31 March 2026 (NZ$(2.891)m FY25), i.e., total liabilities exceed total assets; net tangible assets per share is negative (-7.62 cents). Current liabilities have also exceeded current assets in recent periods (a going-concern disclosure point).

Quoted shares outstanding rose from roughly 53m to 66.4m between FY2022 and FY2026 (plus a prior 15-for-1 share consolidation effective 30 March 2022, when the company was renamed from Cooks Global Foods to Cooks Coffee Company), reflecting repeated reliance on new equity issuance and related-party/cornerstone-investor support to fund the business.

Market capitalisation in the low tens of millions of NZ dollars with thin trading on both NZX and the AQSE London board; management itself describes UK share trading liquidity as "still low" while planning a UK domicile transition to try to fix this.

financial.risk: Absolute profit levels are tiny and highly sensitive to one-offs
financial.description: FY2026 net profit was only NZ$315k (down 61% YoY) and normalised EBITDA is ~NZ$1.7-1.9m; a small swing in bad debts, FX, or one-off costs can move reported profitability by a large percentage.

financial.risk: Lease liabilities dominate the balance sheet
financial.description: IFRS 16 lease liabilities of ~NZ$27.7m dwarf reported borrowings of NZ$2.86m; while offset by matching lease receivables (Cooks subleases premises to franchisees), this creates balance-sheet complexity and interest-rate sensitivity on both sides.

regulatory.description: Simultaneous NZX Main Board and UK AQSE (Aquis) compliance, plus a stated intention to transition domicile to the UK, adds ongoing governance and disclosure cost for a company of this size.

regulatory.risk: Franchise law and employment regulation in multiple jurisdictions
regulatory.description: UK, Ireland and emerging India/UAE/Middle East franchise, food-safety and employment regulations must each be navigated, typically indirectly through franchisees/master franchisees.

macro.description: Coffee-shop spend is discretionary; a UK or Irish consumer slowdown, elevated interest rates, or cost-of-living pressure could reduce like-for-like sales and slow the pace of new franchisee sign-ups.

Coffee bean, dairy, food and UK/Irish labour cost inflation (National Living Wage increases) pressure franchisee unit economics, indirectly threatening royalty income and the appeal of new franchise sign-ups.
Reporting currency is NZD while the overwhelming majority of trading is in GBP and EUR; currency translation adds volatility to reported results independent of underlying trading.

macro_factors.industry_outlook: UK branded coffee-shop market (~£6.1bn, 11,456 stores per Allegra/World Coffee Portal, Jan 2025) projected to grow to £8.1bn by 2030 (5.7% CAGR in value, ~3.0% in store numbers); Irish branded market (768 stores) projected to grow at ~2.4% CAGR in store numbers to 2030. Mature, competitive, consolidated market with strong incumbents.
macro_factors.cyclicality: Moderate — coffee-shop visitation is discretionary but relatively low-ticket/habitual spend that has historically shown some resilience versus big-ticket discretionary categories, though franchisee unit economics are sensitive to input cost and wage inflation cycles
macro_factors.interest_rate_sensitivity: Moderate — company carries bank borrowings (NZ$2.86m) and large offsetting lease assets/liabilities (~NZ$25-28m each side); UK/Irish base rates also affect franchisee financing costs and consumer discretionary spending
key_input_costs: Coffee beans (organic/Fairtrade certified, likely a cost premium)
Commercial rents in UK/Ireland retail locations

recent_developments.event: Announced confirmed new stores committed in Dubai (UAE) and India under the newly signed master franchise agreements, alongside continued UK/Ireland store openings (per the FY27 trading update referenced in the FY2026 annual report: 4 new UK stores, 2 new Irish stores, and 3 new international stores committed as at 23 June 2026).

FY2026 preliminary (unaudited) results announced: revenue up 83.7-87% to NZ$12.358-12.8m (vs NZ$6.7m FY25); EBITDA NZ$1.30-1.39m; net profit from continuing operations NZ$315k (down 61.3% YoY); debt reduced from NZ$4.3m to NZ$2.86m; UK & Ireland network grew 18% to 105 sites (82 UK, 23 Ireland); store sales (system-wide) up 22.8% to NZ$95.8m.

Master Franchise Agreement signed for the United Arab Emirates — 10-year term with renewal right, minimum 50 Esquires outlets committed over the agreement term, with UK-based franchisee-operators as partners.
First Tesco Ireland partnership store opened in Tullamore, County Offaly; four further Tesco in-store Esquires cafes followed by end of January 2026 (Clonmel, Youghal, Waterford, Wexford).

H1 FY2026 (six months to 30 September 2025) results: revenue up 111% to NZ$5.77m, EBITDA NZ$0.61m (down from NZ$0.81m prior year, or -5% normalised), net profit before tax from continuing operations NZ$68k (down from NZ$534k); UK & Ireland store sales up 26.9% to NZ$45.5m; store count 96, rising to 100 by report date.
Master Franchise Agreement signed for India with Sterling Coffee Houses (Special Purpose Vehicle); first India stores expected to open before end of FY2026 (i.e., by March 2026).

guidance.as_of: FY2026 Annual Report / Chairman's Report, 28-29 May 2026

items.period: FY2034 (long-term target, maintained across multiple years)
items.notes: 105 stores at end of FY2026; company reiterates it expects to keep adding stores at a similar annual pace to reach 300 by FY2034.

items.target: 4 new UK stores, 2 new Ireland stores, 3 new international stores committed
items.notes: Described as "the FY27 financial year has begun strongly"; no quantified revenue or EBITDA guidance given for FY2027.
Mallow store only contributed 43 of 52 weeks in FY26; full-year contribution plus potential further Dairygold sites should lift this segment materially, though no numeric target given.

items.target: Sell/appoint Regional Developer rights for Scotland and Northern Ireland
items.period: Originally targeted FY2026 (per H1 FY26 going-concern disclosure); not confirmed as completed in the FY2026 annual report
items.notes: As of the FY2026 annual report, Regional Developers are still described as "currently being sought" for West Midlands, Scotland and Northern Ireland, suggesting the original FY26 target for Scotland/NI was not met on schedule.

guidance.management_commentary: Executive Chairman Keith Jackson: growth in Esquires store numbers and store sales continues to "significantly exceed reported industry growth in both core markets"; the Board "views the future with optimism," citing the Tesco Ireland and Dairygold managed-store partnerships, the new India and UAE master franchise agreements, and the ongoing UK Regional Developer rollout as the basis for continued expansion toward the 300-store FY2034 target. No formal quantitative revenue, EBITDA or profit guidance range was issued for FY2027.

bull_case: Genuine, above-market store and sales growth in both core UK and Irish markets (store growth of 17% UK / 35% Ireland vs. reported industry growth of 3.5% / 2.5%) suggests the franchise concept is resonating and taking incremental share, albeit from a very low base

New high-footfall distribution channels (Tesco Ireland, Dairygold superstores) and new international master-franchise agreements (India, UAE with a 50-store minimum commitment) open large incremental addressable markets at little direct capital cost to Cooks
Balance sheet is de-risking: bank debt cut from NZ$4.3m to NZ$2.86m in FY2026 and debt-to-total-assets down to 8.2%, after several years of losses and going-concern uncertainty

The company has returned to sustained (if small) profitability for two consecutive years (FY2025, FY2026) after a multi-year run of losses driven by legacy impairments and the Triple Two exit, suggesting the core UK/Ireland Esquires franchise model may finally be a stable, cash-generative base

Micro-cap optionality: at a market cap of roughly NZ$15-20m against NZ$95.8m of system-wide store sales and a stated 300-store FY2034 target, any acceleration in royalty capture or a successful scaling of the managed-store/master-franchise model could re-rate the stock materially — though this cuts both ways given the risks below
bear_case: The headline FY2026 revenue growth (83-87%) is substantially a consolidation/mix effect from bringing company-managed Dairygold and Tesco Ireland store sales onto the P&L (Managed Cafes segment revenue rose from NZ$0.987m to NZ$5.317m), not organic franchise royalty growth — system-wide store sales, the more representative operating metric, rose only 22.8%; any DCF or trend analysis using the reported revenue CAGR across this break will materially overstate the business's true growth rate

Negative shareholders' equity (NZ$(2.223)m at FY2026) and a history of going-concern disclosures, repeated equity raises, and reliance on cornerstone/related-party financial support point to a structurally fragile balance sheet for a company of any size, let alone one expanding into new geographies

Absolute profitability remains negligible (NZ$315k FY2026 net profit, down 61% YoY) and highly sensitive to one-off items (bad debts, FX, discontinued-store closures); the business has not yet demonstrated it can compound profit growth, only revenue and store count

Extreme scale disadvantage against Costa Coffee (~38% UK share), Starbucks (~19%) and Caffe Nero (~9%) versus Esquires' own disclosed ~0.8% UK / ~2.5% Irish share limits pricing power, marketing reach, and site-acquisition leverage in an already mature, competitive market

Micro-cap illiquidity across both the NZX and AQSE London listings, a five-year history of heavy losses (FY2018-FY2021 restructuring/COVID losses, then a NZ$2.385m goodwill impairment in FY2023 and a NZ$3.352m discontinued-operations loss in FY2024 from exiting/writing down prior investments including Triple Two Coffee), and a 15-for-1 share consolidation plus share count growth from ~53m to 66.4m (FY2022-FY2026) all point to a chequered capital-markets history that should temper confidence in the recent turnaround being durable
